vt2_papal_states.topic: The Papal States 754-1870: Pepin's donation, the Constantine forgery, extent and government, 1848-49

claims.text: In January 1754 Pope Stephen II met Pippin at Ponthion; at Quierzy in April 754 Pippin promised to restore papal lands taken by the Lombard king Aistulf (no record of the promise survives); Stephen anointed Pippin and his sons in 754.

In 755-756 Pippin invaded Italy, defeated Aistulf, and in 756 the keys of the surrendered cities with a list of them were placed on the altar of Old St Peter's; papal accounts say he granted the exarchate including Ravenna and the Roman duchy, much of it imperial territory to which he had no clear legal claim. Charlemagne and Louis the Pious (817) confirmed it.

The Donation of Constantine purported to record Constantine's grant to Pope Sylvester I of primacy over the great sees and control of the imperial palace in Rome and the regions of the Western Empire; it was composed by an unknown writer in the 8th century (consensus 750s-760s); Leo IX (1049-54) was the first pope to cite it in an official act; Lorenzo Valla demonstrated in 1440 that its Latin was not that of the 4th century.
Britannica dates the Papal States 756-1870, covering modern Lazio, Umbria, Marche and part of Emilia-Romagna.

Cardinal Albornoz promulgated the Constitutiones Aegidianae on 29 April 1357, a uniform civil code in force until 1816; the popes resided at Avignon in the 14th century (1309-1376 per infobox); expansion under Alexander VI and Julius II; Parma and Piacenza annexed 1512.

Major provinces were governed by cardinal legates and the state was run through cardinal-led congregations; Napoleon annexed the Marches on 2 April 1808 and Rome on 17 May 1809; the Congress of Vienna restored the Italian territories but not Avignon; revolts in 1830 and 1848 were suppressed by the Austrian army.
Area before 1859: 44,000 km2; population in 1853: 3,124,668.

In 1860 Piedmont-Sardinia conquered the eastern two-thirds of the Papal States (Bologna, Ferrara, Umbria, the Marches, Benevento, Pontecorvo annexed by November 1860); in March 1861 the first Italian parliament declared Rome the capital; a French garrison protected Pius IX until recalled at the outbreak of the Franco-Prussian War in July 1870.

Papal minister Pellegrino Rossi was assassinated on 15 November 1848; Pius IX fled to Gaeta on the night of 24 November 1848; the Roman Republic was proclaimed on 9 February 1849; triumvirate Armellini, Mazzini, Saffi; its constitution guaranteed freedom of religion and abolished the death penalty; French troops under Oudinot landed 25 April 1849 and entered Rome 3 July 1849; Pius IX returned in April 1850.

vt2_roman_question.topic: 20 September 1870, the Law of Guarantees and the 'prisoner of the Vatican' years, 1870-1929

claims.text: Italy declared war on 10 September 1870 after Pius IX refused Italian troops; the army crossed the frontier on 11 September, breached the walls at Porta Pia and took Rome on 20 September 1870; resistance was token because Pius IX wanted to show Rome was taken by force; a plebiscite followed in October and annexation is dated 9 October 1870.

The Law of Guarantees was passed on 13 May 1871: the pope's person sacred and inviolable, royal honours, an annual endowment of 3,225,000 lire, use of the Vatican and Lateran palaces and Castel Gandolfo, free communication and conclave; it was a domestic law because Catholic governments showed no interest in an international congress.
Pius IX refused the endowment, expressly on 13 November 1872; he and his two successors never touched it and relied on donations.

In Ubi Nos (15 May 1871) Pius IX wrote that he 'never can and never shall allow or accept those guarantees' devised by the Piedmont Government, and that civil rule was given so the pope 'may never be subject to any ruler or civil power'.

From 1870 to 1929 Pius IX, Leo XIII, Pius X, Benedict XV and Pius XI did not leave the Vatican, did not appear on the loggia facing St Peter's Square, and gave Urbi et Orbi blessings facing a courtyard or inside the basilica.

The non expedit (adopted 1868, confirmed by Pius IX 1874) barred Italian Catholics from national political participation ('neither elected nor electors'); largely relaxed by Pius X in 1904-05; formally lifted by Benedict XV in 1919, who approved the PPI.
On 25 July 1929 Pius XI led a procession in St Peter's Square; the New York Times (26 July 1929, Arnaldo Cortesi) reported he left the Vatican for the first time in 59 years before 300,000 people.

vt2_pacts_signed.topic: The Lateran Pacts of 11 February 1929: motives, negotiators, the three instruments, the money, the PPI and Catholic Action; control then and now

claims.text: The Treaty was signed in Rome on 11 February 1929 by Cardinal Pietro Gasparri, Secretary of State, plenipotentiary of Pius XI, and Benito Mussolini, Prime Minister and Head of Government, plenipotentiary of King Victor Emmanuel III; ratifications exchanged in the Apostolic Palace on 7 June 1929. Treaty 27 articles; Concordat 45 articles.

Treaty Art. 1: the Catholic religion 'is the sole religion of the State'; Art. 2: Italy recognizes the sovereignty of the Holy See in the international field 'as an attribute inherent to its nature'; Art. 3: full ownership and exclusive and absolute sovereign power and jurisdiction over Vatican City; Art. 4: no interference by the Italian government; Arts 13-16: ownership and diplomatic-style immunities of the Lateran and other basilicas and Castel Gandolfo; Art. 21: cardinals receive honours of princes of the blood; Art. 22: Italy punishes crimes committed in Vatican City at the Holy See's request.

Treaty Art. 24: the Holy See 'wishes to remain and will remain extraneous to temporal competitions between other States'; Vatican City 'always and in every case considered neutral and inviolable territory'.

Treaty Art. 26: the Holy See declares the Roman Question 'definitively and irrevocably settled and therefore eliminated' and recognizes the Kingdom of Italy under the House of Savoy with Rome as capital; the law of 13 May 1871 n. 214 is repealed.

Financial Convention Art. 1: Italy pays the Holy See 750,000,000 lire on the exchange of ratifications and delivers 5% bearer Consolidated Italian bonds of nominal value 1,000,000,000 lire; Art. 2: accepted as the definitive settlement of financial relations 'in dependence on the events of 1870'; preamble: the Pope limited the request to the strictly necessary, considering the State's finances and the economic conditions of the Italian people especially after the war, a sum much lower than what the State would have owed under the law of 13 May 1871.

Concordat Art. 34 gives civil effects to sacramental marriage governed by canon law; Art. 36 makes Catholic doctrine the foundation and crown of public instruction; Art. 43 recognizes Azione Cattolica organizations acting outside any political party and bars clergy and religious from enrolling in any political party.
Pius XI, 13 February 1929, to the Università Cattolica: 'perhaps also a man was needed like the one Providence has caused us to meet'; the pacts had 'given God back to Italy and Italy to God'.

Pius XI, 11 February 1929, to Rome's parish priests: the territory requested was 'very little, very very little, the least possible', likened to the amount of body needed to keep the soul together; the Holy See has the right to provide for its economic independence.

Francesco Pacelli (b. 1874), lawyer and brother of Eugenio Pacelli (later Pius XII), led the negotiations from 1926 at Pius XI's wish; kept a 'Diario della Conciliazione' (published 1959); made marquis and general counsellor of Vatican City State; drafted the new state's first laws (7 June 1929) with jurist Federico Cammeo.
Francesco Pacelli had over two hundred audiences with Pius XI on some twenty successive drafts; made hereditary marquess by brief of 9 June 1929.

The Pacts are three instruments: the Treaty (settled the Roman Question, created Vatican City State), the Concordat (the Church's life in Italy) and the Financial Convention (compensation for the loss of the Papal States); the Concordat was revised in 1984 while the Treaty remained substantially unchanged (Dalla Torre).

Kertzer (NPR, 2014): Mussolini, a committed anticleric, came to see the importance of enlisting the pope's support; the Church lent the regime organizational strength and moral legitimacy; Pius XI saw Mussolini as the best bet to prevent a socialist takeover; the Church gained state payments to clergy, chaplains in fascist youth groups, religion in schools.

Pollard (1999): the Pacts gave the Vatican a substantial capital endowment; Pius XI entrusted its investment to Bernardino Nogara; losses within two years were attributed to ambitious spending, weak controls and the 1929 crash.

The Special Administration of the Holy See was created by Pius XI on 7 June 1929 to manage the Financial Convention funds, reporting directly to the pope; Nogara ran it 1929-1954; merged into APSA in 1967.

The PPI was founded on 18 January 1919 (Sturzo); 20.5% and 100 seats in 1919, 20.4% and 108 seats in 1921; dissolved 5 November 1926; historian John Molony argued the fascist state and the Vatican 'worked hand in hand' to help destroy it.

Sturzo resigned as PPI leader on 10 July 1923 after consulting the Holy See, following Mussolini's threats of reprisals against the clergy; Pius XI's stance was ambiguous; Gasparri arranged his emigration; he left for London on 25 October 1924.

The 'leggi fascistissime' of 5 November 1926 made the PNF the sole party ('P.N.F. unico partito'), suppressed freedom of association and press, created a special tribunal and restored the death penalty.

In Non abbiamo bisogno (29 June 1931) Pius XI protested the police dissolution of Catholic youth and university associations, accused the regime of seeking to monopolize the young and of 'a real pagan worship of the State', and called the fascist oath as it stood unlawful.

Francis promulgated a new Fundamental Law of Vatican City State on 13 May 2023, in force 7 June 2023, replacing John Paul II's 2000 law, which had replaced Pius XI's 1929 law; only the pope holds powers, bodies exercise functions.

Leo XIV promulgated a further Fundamental Law dated 31 July 2026: Pontifical Commission of cardinals and other members appointed for five years; pope appoints the Governorate's president and judges; Governorate headed by Sr Raffaella Petrini.
Robert Francis Prevost was elected the 267th pope, Leo XIV, on 8 May 2025.
